docs.title: Talk to ATC. It talks back.
docs.text:
Hold push-to-talk and speak as you would on a real radio. A controller answers in US FAA phraseology, on the frequency you are tuned to, from the gate at one airport to the gate at the next.

Get started What ATC can do

YouSeattle Clearance, November 547 Golf Alpha, IFR to Portland with Charlie.

ClearanceN547GA, cleared to Portland via the SUMMA2 departure, then as filed. Maintain 5000, expect 16000 10 minutes after departure. Departure frequency 119.2, squawk 4521.

YouCleared to Portland, SUMMA2 then as filed, 5000 expect 16000, 119.2, squawk 4521, 547GA. ✓ Readback accepted

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• Every position talks to you

    Clearance Delivery, Ground, Tower, Departure, Center and Approach, each on its real frequency. Tune a frequency nobody is on and you hear nothing.

    What ATC can do

  • Real procedures

    IFR clearances, taxi routes with hold shorts, SIDs and STARs, climbs and descents, vectors to an ILS, RNAV or visual approach, and handoffs in between.

    A flight, gate to gate

  • Readbacks are checked

    A correct readback gets silence and a check mark. A wrong one is corrected: "negative, squawk six six six two".

    Readbacks

  • ATC calls you first

    Handoffs, a readback you forgot, an altitude you drifted from, traffic, a go-around: the controller speaks when a real one would.

    At every position

  • ATC's plan, drawn

    When Approach vectors you, the window draws the whole plan: the downwind, the base turn, where you join the final, and you.

    The approach plan

  • Any US airport

    Procedures, frequencies and airspace from the FAA's own data. Taxiways and parking from your own X-Plane scenery.

    Your X-Plane's data

docs.title: What a flight is like
docs.text:
1. Start X-Plane 12 and the xatc-agent window. Press New flight and enter your flight plan, or load it from SimBrief.
  2. Tune the ATIS and listen. Then call Clearance Delivery, get your clearance and read it back.
  3. Ground taxis you to the runway. Tower clears you for takeoff. Departure climbs you and puts you on course. Center takes you to cruise and brings you down again.
  4. Approach vectors you to final and clears the approach. Tower clears you to land and tells you where to leave the runway. Ground taxis you to the parking you ask for.

Your first flight walks through it step by step.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• X-Plane 12 on Windows

    X-Plane 12.1.4 or newer, Windows 10 or 11, a microphone, and an internet connection during the flight. The controller runs in the cloud; the window beside X-Plane is a thin client.

  • An invitation

    xatc-agent is an invitation-only experiment. The owner creates your account and gives you the client.

    Install and sign in

docs.title: Know before you fly
docs.text:
A simulation, and an experiment

xatc-agent is for flight simulation only. It is not a training device and must never be used for real-world flying. It is under active development: what a controller says and does changes between releases, and things break.

  • IFR only, for now. VFR departures, pattern work and flight following are not built.
  • US airports work best: everything outside the taxiways comes from the FAA's data. Outside the US, ATC asks your X-Plane for the airport's procedures and frequencies instead.
  • English, FAA phraseology.
  • When ATC is asked for something it has not been taught, it says so: "unable, I have not completed that training." It does not make something up.

All the known limitations are on one page.

docs.title: Your first flight
docs.text: An IFR flight from Seattle to Portland, gate to gate. The frequencies and names are examples: the window's Frequencies card lists the real ones for your flight.

docs.title: Before you call anyone
docs.text:
1. Start X-Plane 12 and put your aircraft on a stand at the departure airport.
  2. Start the client and wait for the startup dialog to close (signed in, gateway ready).
  3. Press New flight.
    • Enter manually: callsign, aircraft type, departure, destination, cruise altitude and route. The dialog remembers your last plan.
    • From SimBrief: enter your SimBrief username or pilot ID and press Load. It fills in your latest flight plan and tells you which one it loaded and how old it is. No password or key is needed.
  4. Press Start flight. The dialog says Starting new flight… and closes when ATC is ready.

The first flight after installing takes longer

The first time, the client reads the headers of your X-Plane scenery once, so it can answer ATC's questions about taxiways and parking. The dialog shows a progress bar. On a slow disk this can take a minute or more. After that, only new or updated scenery is read.

docs.title: How to talk
docs.text:
• Push-to-talk: hold the big button in the window, hold Space while the window has focus, or use a yoke or joystick button (Settings).
  • You transmit on the COM radio selected on your aircraft's audio panel, on its active frequency. The push-to-talk button names who is listening there.
  • Say who you are calling, your callsign, and what you want, as on a real radio. Read back clearances and instructions.
  • You hear ATC only if COM1 or COM2 is tuned to the frequency ATC transmits on.
  • While X-Plane is paused, ATC is silent and does not hear you.

docs.title: 1. ATIS
docs.text: Tune the ATIS frequency on either radio. The recording loops, starting mid-broadcast like the real thing. Note the information letter and the altimeter.

docs.title: 2. Clearance Delivery
docs.text:
You: Seattle Clearance, November five four seven Golf Alpha, IFR to Portland with information Charlie.

ATC: November five four seven Golf Alpha, cleared to Portland via the Summa Two departure, then as filed. Maintain five thousand, expect one six thousand one zero minutes after departure. Departure frequency one one niner point two, squawk four five two one.

You: Cleared to Portland, Summa Two then as filed, five thousand expect one six thousand, one one niner point two, squawk four five two one, five four seven Golf Alpha.

ATC: November five four seven Golf Alpha, readback correct.

Prefer not to copy a clearance by voice? Request a PDC and it arrives as text.

docs.title: 3. Ground
docs.text:
You: Seattle Ground, November five four seven Golf Alpha, at alpha eleven, ready to taxi with Charlie.

Ground gives you a route along your scenery's real taxiways, with a hold short for each runway on the way. Read back the runway and every hold short. Ask for a pushback first if you need one. If you get lost, say "request progressive taxi" and Ground calls each turn as you come up to it.

docs.title: 4. Tower
docs.text: At the hold line, the window shows Next: Seattle Tower with buttons that put the frequency in a radio's standby. Call ready. Tower may line you up and wait, hold you for traffic or wake turbulence, or clear you for takeoff with the wind and your initial heading or RNAV fix.

docs.title: 5. Departure and Center
docs.text:
About 1,000 ft above the ground, Tower hands you to Departure. Check in with your altitude:

You: Seattle Departure, November five four seven Golf Alpha, one thousand two hundred climbing five thousand.

Departure says "radar contact", climbs you and turns you on course. Center takes over on the way up and, later, starts your descent: "descend via the Helns Six arrival", or a crossing restriction. Along the way you can ask for another altitude, direct to a fix on your route, or a deviation around weather.

docs.title: 6. Approach
docs.text:
Approach tells you which approach to expect and vectors you to final. The first vector says why: "..., vectors for the ILS runway one zero right". ATC does not say the pattern it plans: the window's Approach card draws it, and the top line of the window confirms that ATC is vectoring you.

ATC: November five four seven Golf Alpha, turn left heading one three zero, maintain three thousand until established, cleared ILS runway one zero right approach.

Read back the heading, the altitude and the approach with its runway. Approach then hands you to Tower.

docs.title: 7. Tower, landing and taxi-in
docs.text: Tower clears you to land with the wind. Read back "cleared to land" with the runway. On the rollout Tower tells you where to turn off, then hands you to Ground. Tell Ground where you are parking: a gate, an FBO, or "general aviation". If ATC asks "say parking", the window's Parking card lists the names you can say and shows them on a map.

docs.title: 8. The end of the flight
docs.text: Park at your stand and shut down the engines. The flight ends by itself within about a minute. You can also press End flight, and closing X-Plane ends the flight after 30 seconds.

docs.title: If something goes wrong
docs.text:
• Silence after you transmit? The log's No reply line says why. See Troubleshooting.
  • Missed what ATC said? Say "say again". The words are also in the log.
  • Closed the client mid-flight by accident? Start it again within about ten minutes and choose Rejoin last flight.

docs.title: Install and sign in
docs.text: xatc-agent has two parts. The controller runs in the cloud. On your sim PC you run a small program, the client, in its own window beside X-Plane. It reads your aircraft's state from X-Plane, sends your voice while you hold push-to-talk, and plays ATC's replies through a radio effect.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
Simulator X-Plane 12.1.4 or newer. The client uses X-Plane's own Web API, and needs the version of it that arrived in 12.1.4. Tested on 12.4.3. Use the current X-Plane 12 release PC Windows 10 or 11. The window uses Edge WebView2, which ships with both Audio A microphone, and speakers or a headset Account An xatc-agent account, created for you by the project owner The client The client package, also from the owner Phone An authenticator app, for the sign-in's second step

Invitation only

xatc-agent is an experiment and is not open for sign-up. If you were invited, the owner has sent you the client and an email with a temporary password.

docs.title: Install (one time)
docs.text:
1. Unzip the client package on the sim PC, anywhere you like.

  2. Open PowerShell in that folder and run:

    powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\setup-windows.ps1

    The script checks for uv (it shows the official install command and asks before running it), installs Python and the client, and runs a quick self-check: the window engine, your audio devices, and whether a sign-in is already saved. It makes no network call.

  3. Allow the microphone: Windows Settings > Privacy & security > Microphone > Let desktop apps access your microphone.

There is nothing else to install and no keys to copy. You sign in from the window.

docs.title: Start the client
docs.text:
Double-click scripts\xatc-agent-client-run.cmd. A console window shows warnings and errors, and the xatc-agent window opens with the startup dialog: one row each for your sign-in, the ATC gateway and X-Plane.

  • X-Plane is shown but not required yet. Start it whenever you like; the client keeps looking for it.
  • Only one client runs at a time. Starting it again brings the window that is already open to the front.

docs.title: Sign in
docs.text:
1. Press Sign in in the startup dialog. Your browser opens the xatc-agent sign-in page.
  2. The first time, enter your email and the temporary password from your invitation, choose your own password, and set up your authenticator app. After that it is your email, your password and the authenticator's code (or a passkey, if you add one).
  3. The browser says Signed in and you can close the tab. The window's sign-in pill turns green.

You stay signed in for 30 days, across restarts. In the last 24 hours the window offers Sign in again, which never interrupts a flight. The client keeps your sign-in in Windows Credential Manager, never in a file.

docs.title: Choose your audio
docs.text:
ATC's address comes with your account. When you sign in, the client gets it. The ATC section of Settings has one line about it: From your account. once the client has it.

  1. Open the Settings view (the startup dialog closes by itself once you are signed in).
  2. Under Audio, pick your microphone and your speakers or headset.
  3. Press Save.

If the line says the address could not be fetched, press Try again.

That is all the setup. Settings describes everything else you can change, such as push-to-talk on a yoke button and how the controllers sound.

docs.title: The recording question
docs.text:
The first time you connect, the window asks one thing before you can transmit:

Keep your radio audio to improve xatc? xatc can keep recordings of what you say on the radio, to train it to understand pilots better. Only your own transmissions are kept, in private storage, for 180 days. The owner and the ATC expert can listen to them. You can change this at any time in Settings. Nothing is kept unless you allow it.

Choose Allow or Don't allow. Your choice is remembered with your account, and you can change it in Settings > Audio. Your data says what else is sent and kept.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Your first flight.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Two parts: a thin client on your sim PC, and the controller in the cloud. One encrypted connection joins them for the whole flight.

How the parts of xatc-agent work together On your PC, X-Plane 12 gives the xatc-agent client the aircraft's state, and the client tunes X-Plane's radios; your microphone and headset carry your voice in and ATC's audio out. The client signs in through your browser with the sign-in service, then keeps one encrypted connection per flight to the voice gateway in the cloud. It sends the aircraft's state, your voice and answers about your scenery, and receives ATC's audio and text, the approach plan and parking. In the gateway, speech recognition hears the call, an AI model understands it, the controller agent (an AI model) decides which ATC tool to use, the tool checks the request and writes the phraseology, and text to speech speaks it. Monitors watch every frame and start ATC's own calls through the same tools. The tools read the FAA's data. Each flight is written to a flight log that is reviewed afterwards. Your PC The cloud X-Plane 12 your aircraft, weather, traffic, scenery xatc-agent client push-to-talk, radios, the cards plays ATC through a radio effect Microphone and headset aircraft state radio tuning your voice ATC audio Sign-in service knows which pilot is flying sign in, in your browser aircraft state your voice, while you hold push-to-talk answers about your scenery, when asked one encrypted connection per flight ATC's audio and text the approach plan parking, frequencies Voice gateway one isolated session per flight Hear speech to text Understand reads the call Decide picks a tool ATC tools check, phrase Speak text to speech Monitors watch every frame, call you first ATC's own calls A readback is judged by the AI model, item by item; code checks every quote against what you said. The FAA's data procedures, frequencies, airspace, altitudes Flight log reviewed after an AI model plain code: it checks, and it writes ATC's words data How the parts work together. The AI model understands and chooses; plain code checks the request and writes what ATC says.

docs.title: One radio call
docs.text:
1. You key the mic. The client streams your audio while push-to-talk is held, beside a frame of aircraft state about once a second.
  2. Speech recognition turns the audio into text. It is tuned for aviation phraseology.
  3. Plain code checks the basics: is a controller on that frequency, and did your callsign come through.
  4. An AI model reads the call. Is it a readback of what ATC just said, a request, or both?
  5. A readback is judged item by item, quoting your own words. Code refuses any quote that is not in the transcript, then decides: accept in silence, correct one item, or ask once for a safety item.
  6. A request goes to the controller agent, an AI model that plays the position you called. Its job is to pick the right tool for what you asked: issue a taxi clearance, assign an altitude, clear an approach.
  7. The tool does the controlling. It checks the request against the FAA's data, your scenery and the state of your flight, writes the exact phraseology, and refuses in fixed words when the data says no.
  8. Text to speech speaks it, the client adds the radio effect, and you hear it if you are tuned to that frequency.

Meanwhile monitors watch every frame of your aircraft's state and start ATC's own calls: handoffs, readback reminders, an altitude that drifted, traffic.

docs.title: Where the AI is, and where it is not
docs.text:
The AI model understands what you said and chooses what kind of thing a controller would do next. It does not invent the clearance.

The model does Code does Classifies your transmission Decides whether a controller is listening on that frequency Judges a readback against what was said Checks that every quoted word was really in your transmission Picks the tool for your request Checks the request against the data: runways, procedures, minimum altitudes, traffic Writes the words ATC speaks, in standard phraseology Watches your flight and starts ATC's own calls

A model can still pick the wrong tool. When it does, the tool refuses rather than issue something the data does not support, and the cost is a retry or an "unable", not a wrong clearance. When no tool fits, ATC says "unable, I have not completed that training".

docs.title: The data
docs.text:
• The FAA's published data, updated every 28-day cycle: procedures (SIDs, STARs, approaches), fixes and airways, facility frequencies and hours, airspace boundaries, minimum vectoring and minimum IFR altitudes.
  • Your X-Plane, asked when needed: taxiways, stands and runway use, and the weather and traffic around you. See Your X-Plane's data.

docs.title: One session per flight
docs.text: Each flight gets its own isolated session in the cloud, which keeps the flight's state: your clearance, where you are in the flight, what you still owe a readback for. It survives a reconnect, and it stops when the flight ends.

docs.title: Why it takes a moment to answer
docs.text: Each reply involves speech recognition, one or two model calls, and speech synthesis. Expect a few seconds from releasing push-to-talk to the first word. The log's Timing line shows each step.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
xatc is an invitation-only experiment under active development. These are the edges as of 2026-10-13; each will be removed from this page when it is fixed.

  • IFR only. Every flight is an IFR flight. VFR departures, pattern work, flight following and VFR arrivals are not built.
  • The United States first. The FAA's data covers the US only. Elsewhere ATC works from your X-Plane's own navigation data for the airport's procedures, fixes and frequencies, and it has no airspace boundaries, Center sectors or minimum vectoring altitudes for the area, so expect less of it there. The project has not flown outside the US. See Your X-Plane's data.
  • Windows, and X-Plane 12.1.4 or newer. The client is a Windows 10 or 11 app and talks to X-Plane through its own Web API. X-Plane has had that API since 12.1.1, and the client needs the version of it that arrived in 12.1.4. Laminar is still extending it release by release, so use the current X-Plane 12. Tested on 12.4.3. There is no macOS or Linux client, and it does not work with X-Plane 11 or other simulators. With an older X-Plane 12 the client shows X-Plane: not connected: see X-Plane too old.
  • The X-Plane data pack replaces the FAA procedure file. ATC flies the FAA's procedures of the current cycle. Settings > X-Plane data can install them into X-Plane's Custom Data folder so your aircraft's FMS and ATC agree. While the pack is installed, X-Plane's own GPS shows the FAA's procedures too, and Remove puts your files back. See FAA procedures for your X-Plane.
  • Clearances by phone at fields without a tower. At an airport with no control tower and no radio way to reach Clearance Delivery, the Frequencies card has a Clearance Delivery · by phone row instead of a frequency. You call the overlying approach control (or the Center) from the window, on the ground only, never Flight Service. The clearance ends with "hold for release": you call back when you are number one for departure and are given a release with a void time.
  • Some replies are still intermittent. In a small number of situations the controller answers correctly most of the time, but not every time. The list shrinks with each release.
  • Controller voices. All the voices are synthetic and speak American English; the radio voices add regional American accents. Settings > Audio has four choices for ATC voices: the radio voices, which give each controller a distinct voice and already sound like a radio, and three standard voices from the most robotic to the most natural. See Settings.
  • Fix names. ATC says a VOR by its name. It says a fix the way controllers say it where a real source confirms it, which so far is a few. Any other fix it says as written ("PANGL" as "Pangl") rather than guess. If a name sounds wrong to you, report it with the time.
  • One client per PC. Starting the client again brings the window that is already open to the front.

docs.title: If you hit something that is not here
docs.text: Say what you said, what you expected and the time, and send the log file: see Reporting a problem.

docs.title: Your data
docs.text: What the client sends, what is kept, and what stays on your PC. This page describes how the software works. It is not a legal agreement. xatc-agent is an invitation-only experiment; ask the project owner about anything this page does not answer.

docs.title: Your account
docs.text:
You sign in with an xatc-agent account that the owner creates for you: your email address, a password you choose, and an authenticator app or a passkey.

  • The client never sees your password. You type it into the sign-in page in your own browser.
  • The client keeps your sign-in in Windows Credential Manager, for up to 30 days. It is never written to a file.
  • ATC knows which account is flying. A flight belongs to the pilot who started it, and nobody else can rejoin it.
  • Sign out removes the sign-in from your PC and cancels it with the sign-in service.

docs.title: What the client sends during a flight
docs.text:
Over one encrypted connection to ATC, for as long as a flight is running:

What When Your flight plan: callsign, aircraft type, departure, destination, cruise altitude, route When the flight starts Your aircraft's state: position, altitude, speed, heading, radios, on the ground or not About once a second The weather at your aircraft and X-Plane's clock Every few seconds The other aircraft in your X-Plane (the nearest 32) About once a second Your microphone Only while you hold push-to-talk Answers to ATC's questions about your scenery: an airport's taxiways and stands When ATC asks. See Your X-Plane's data

No connection to ATC is open when no flight is running, and your microphone is never sent outside push-to-talk.

docs.title: What happens to your voice
docs.text:
While you hold push-to-talk, your audio is streamed to a speech recognition service and turned into text. The text is what ATC works from.

When the client's Speech recognition setting is Scribe, the audio of your transmissions goes to a third-party speech service outside xatc's own systems, to be written down. When it is Standard, or if that service cannot be reached, xatc's own speech recognition writes it down within xatc's systems.

The full statement, which names the services, is the Privacy page on the pilot site.

docs.title: Recordings of your voice
docs.text:
By default nothing you say is kept as audio. The first time you connect, the window asks:

Keep your radio audio to improve xatc? xatc can keep recordings of what you say on the radio, to train it to understand pilots better. Only your own transmissions are kept, in private storage, for 180 days. The owner and the ATC expert can listen to them. You can change this at any time in Settings. Nothing is kept unless you allow it.

  • You must choose Allow or Don't allow before you can transmit.
  • The choice is stored with your account, so you are asked once, not once per PC.
  • Change it at any time in Settings > Audio.

docs.title: What is kept about a flight
docs.text:
Each flight is logged so that it can be reviewed and the controller improved:

  • what you said, as text, and what ATC answered,
  • what ATC decided,
  • your aircraft's track,
  • which account flew it.

The project owner and an air traffic control expert who advises the project review flights in a private tool. They can see the items above, and they can listen to your recordings only if you allowed them.

docs.title: Other services
docs.text:
• The AI model. The text of your transmissions, with the facts of your flight, is processed by an AI model to work out what you asked for and to judge readbacks. See How it works.
  • SimBrief. If you load a flight plan from SimBrief, the client fetches your latest plan from SimBrief with the username or pilot ID you typed. No SimBrief password or key is involved.

docs.title: What stays on your PC
docs.text:
• Settings: ATC's address (written from your account's answer, never shown in the window, and recorded in the log file), your SimBrief username or pilot ID, your X-Plane folder, your last flight plan. No password and no key.
  • The log file: connections, ATC's address, what ATC asked of your X-Plane, warnings and errors. Never your sign-in and never audio.
  • The window answers only to your own PC. No website can press your push-to-talk, sign you in or sign you out.
  • Your X-Plane files are read, never uploaded as files. The only writes are the optional FAA procedures, which you install and remove yourself.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Everything is configured on the window's Settings view. There are no command-line options to learn and no files to edit. The view has two tabs: General and X-Plane data.

Save checks every field first. A bad value is highlighted and nothing is saved. With a flight under way, Save reconnects on the same flight with the new settings, waiting for ATC to finish talking first. Save never starts a flight.

docs.title: ATC
docs.text:
Setting What it is ATC address One line, not a field. ATC's address comes with your account when you sign in. The line says From your account. once the client has it, and the window never shows the address itself. If it could not be fetched, the line says so and Try again is beside it Sign-in service Two values that come with the client. Change them only when the owner tells you to

While a flight is up, this section also shows the flight's session id.

docs.title: Simulator
docs.text: Setting What it is Aircraft state from X-Plane 12 is the normal choice. Replay a recording and None (a fixed aircraft parked at Seattle) are for testing without the sim X-Plane host and Web API port Where X-Plane's Web API listens. The default, 127.0.0.1 and 8086, is right when the client runs on the same PC as X-Plane Silence X-Plane's own ATIS and AWOS during a flight On by default. X-Plane has an ATIS and AWOS of its own on the same frequencies, so with both on you would hear two voices with two sets of weather. During a flight the client switches X-Plane's off and switches it back on when the flight ends. If you had it off already, it stays off End the flight when X-Plane is closed for Seconds. The default is 30. A pause or a stutter never ends a flight. 0 turns it off

docs.title: Push-to-talk
docs.text:
The window's button and the Space key always work. Also transmit with adds one more:

Choice What it does Only this window The button, or hold Space while the window has focus Enter in the console window Each press toggles transmitting on or off A yoke or joystick button, through X-Plane Hold the button to transmit, wherever the focus is

For a yoke or joystick button, press Learn button, then press and release the button you want within 10 seconds. X-Plane must be running. The client reads the button through X-Plane, so anything X-Plane sees as a joystick button works.

docs.title: Audio
docs.text: Setting Choices Use the microphone and speakers Off: no microphone and no sound, for testing Microphone, Speakers / headset Your devices, or the system default. A headset switched on after the client started appears after Refresh devices Radio effect Clean, Realistic or Busy day: how much of a VHF radio you hear on ATC's voice ATC voices The voices ATC speaks with. Four choices, in this order: Radio voices: distinct controllers with accents, then under Standard voices: Standard (the most robotic), Neural (the default) and Generative (the most natural, and may be slightly slower to start). Saving a change reconnects the flight (the same flight), so ATC switches at once Speech recognition How your transmissions are written down for ATC. Two choices: Standard (the default) and Scribe, which knows your flight's names. Saving a change reconnects the flight (the same flight); it applies from your next transmission. If Scribe is not available on a flight, Settings says Scribe is not available on this flight: speech recognition is Standard. See Your data for where the audio goes ATC delivery How briskly controllers talk: Relaxed, Brisk (the default, about 15% faster) or Fast (about 30% faster). The ATIS is always read at the relaxed pace The recording choice Your answer to the recording question, with Allow and Don't allow to change it. See Your data

docs.title: The radio voices
docs.text: The radio voices are off by default. With them on, each controller on the radio gets a distinct voice with an accent. Within a flight, one frequency keeps one voice. They already sound like a radio, so the Radio effect only adds its key-up click and tail to them. Phone calls, the ATIS and AWOS keep the Neural voices. If the radio voices are not available on a flight, the flight goes on with the standard voices, and Settings says so under the list.

docs.title: Display
docs.text: Setting What it is Theme Dark (the default) or light. The sun/moon button in the header switches it too Show the Approach card On by default. Off, the window never shows ATC's approach plan as a card. The confirmation in the header still shows

docs.title: X-Plane data
docs.text:
The second tab.

Setting What it is X-Plane folder Leave blank to use the folder X-Plane last ran from FAA procedures and ATC data for X-Plane Installs the FAA's current procedures into your X-Plane, and takes them out again. See Your X-Plane's data

docs.title: Where things are kept
docs.text:
What Where (Windows) Settings %LOCALAPPDATA%\xatc-agent-client\settings.json The log file %LOCALAPPDATA%\xatc-agent-client\logs\xatc-agent-client.log Your sign-in Windows Credential Manager, under xatc-agent-client. Never in a file

The Settings view shows both paths at the bottom, with Open log folder.

The settings file never holds a password or a key. It holds ATC's address (written from your account's answer, never by the window, and never shown in it), the sign-in service's two public values, your SimBrief username or pilot ID, your X-Plane folder, and your last flight plan, which pre-fills the New flight dialog.

The log file rotates at 5 MB and keeps five older files. It has every connect and disconnect, ATC's address, what ATC asked of your X-Plane, and every warning and error. It never has your sign-in or any audio. Send it along when you report a problem.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Start with the log at the bottom of the window. It says why something did not happen.

If something is simply not built yet, it is on the known limitations page.

docs.title: ATC does not answer
docs.text:
After a transmission with no reply, the log has a No reply line with the reason:

Reason What it means What to do no_controller_on_frequency Nobody works the frequency you transmitted on Check which radio is selected to transmit (TX), and its active frequency. The Frequencies card lists the right ones sim_paused X-Plane is paused Unpause. ATC is silent and deaf while paused sim_in_replay X-Plane is in a replay Leave the replay empty_transcript The speech recognition heard nothing Check your microphone (below) agent_chose_silence ATC judged that no reply was needed Normal after a correct readback or a remark. Look for the ✓ Readback accepted busy ATC was still handling your previous call Wait a moment and say it again error Something failed Say it again. If it repeats, send the log file

If ATC answers "Aircraft calling, say again", it did not catch your callsign. Say your full callsign clearly.

docs.title: I cannot hear ATC
docs.text:
• You hear ATC only on a frequency you are tuned to. If the log says a reply was "not played (not tuned)", COM1 or COM2 was not on that frequency.
  • ATC's audio waits while you are transmitting. Release push-to-talk.
  • Check Settings > Audio > Speakers / headset. A headset you switched on after the client started appears after Refresh devices.

docs.title: The log shows nothing after "You:"
docs.text:
Your microphone is not reaching the client.

  • Windows Settings > Privacy & security > Microphone: allow desktop apps.
  • Settings > Audio > Microphone: pick the right device.
  • Push-to-talk releases when the window loses focus. To transmit while X-Plane has focus, use a yoke or joystick button.

docs.title: X-Plane: not connected
docs.text:
• The client and X-Plane must run on the same PC. X-Plane's Web API listens only on 127.0.0.1:8086.
  • Check Settings > Simulator: X-Plane 12, host 127.0.0.1, port 8086.
  • The client keeps looking every few seconds. You do not need to restart it after starting X-Plane.

docs.title: X-Plane too old
docs.text:
The client needs X-Plane 12.1.4 or newer. It uses X-Plane's own Web API, and needs the version of it that arrived in 12.1.4.

  • Client 0.13.0 or newer: the X-Plane pill reads X-Plane: too old, with "X-Plane 12.1.4 or newer is needed; this is 12.1.2" (the version your X-Plane reports), or "X-Plane 12.1.4 or newer is needed; this one is older" when your X-Plane is too old to say which version it is. When X-Plane is connected, the window's header shows its version after the client's.
  • A client older than 0.13.0: an older X-Plane 12 does not answer the client's first question, so the client treats it as not there. The startup dialog and the window show X-Plane: not connected, with "not reachable at 127.0.0.1:8086; retrying", and the console window says "X-Plane not reachable". It does not go away, however long you wait, and it looks like X-Plane: not connected, whose checks do not help.

What to do: update X-Plane 12 to the current release.

docs.title: Tower will not clear me
docs.text:
• Traffic. Tower waits for a departure ahead to be clear, and for an arrival on short final. It tells you why.
  • Wake turbulence. Behind a heavy, the wait is two or three minutes: "expect departure in two minutes".
  • No traffic data. If the client loses X-Plane's traffic feed, Tower holds every takeoff and landing clearance until it is back, because it cannot see the runway. A multiplayer or traffic plugin that takes over X-Plane's traffic can cause this.

docs.title: Unable to access data, check connection
docs.text:
A red alert, and X-Plane is paused for you. ATC could not read its airport and procedure data, so it cannot control safely.

  • Check your internet connection.
  • When the data is back, the alert clears by itself and the log says "Data access restored". X-Plane stays paused until you unpause it.

docs.title: Update the client
docs.text: "Update the client to x.y.z or newer": ATC needs a newer client than yours and has stopped connecting. Install the newer client package from the owner and start again.

docs.title: Sign-in
docs.text: You see What to do Not signed in Press Sign in. A sign-in lasts 30 days Signed in · offline The sign-in service cannot be reached. Your flight keeps going and the client keeps trying "Your sign-in expires in ..." Press Sign in again whenever it suits you. It does not interrupt a flight "This flight belongs to another pilot" You tried to rejoin a flight another account started. Press New flight "Your account isn't allowed to fly" Ask the owner "Can't confirm this flight's pilot right now. Retrying." Nothing to do. The client reconnects by itself and your flight is kept

docs.title: The window
docs.text:
• It opened in my browser instead. The window needs Edge WebView2, which ships with Windows 10 and 11. Without it the same page opens in your default browser and works the same.
  • "Already running". Only one client runs at a time. Starting it again brings the window that is already open to the front (a client older than 0.13.0 says it cannot start: use the window that is open).
  • I closed the client mid-flight. Start it again within about ten minutes and choose Rejoin last flight.

docs.title: The radios will not tune from the window
docs.text: The 1, 2 and ⇄ buttons write to X-Plane. They are greyed out while X-Plane is not connected; hover over them for the reason. Only real VHF COM frequencies are accepted (118.000 to 136.990 MHz).

docs.title: Reporting a problem
docs.text:
Check the known limitations first. Then send the owner:

  1. What you said and what you expected, with the time.
  2. The log file: Settings, at the bottom, Open log folder. It never contains your sign-in or any audio.

docs.title: The window
docs.text:
The client runs in its own window, titled xatc-agent, beside X-Plane. It has two views, Radio and Settings. This page is a tour of the Radio view, from the top.

On the ground at Seattle, just after Ground's taxi instruction: the Read back line shows what ATC is waiting for.

docs.title: The header
docs.text:
• Your flight: callsign, aircraft type, departure → destination, and its state (starting, ready, ended). With no flight it says "No flight: press New flight". When a flight ended, the line under it says why.
  • The approach confirmation: while ATC has you on an approach, a pill beside your callsign shows the kind of approach (ILS, RNAV, Visual), the runway, and ATC is vectoring you. It turns green and says cleared for the approach once ATC clears you. See The approach plan.
  • End flight (only while a flight runs) and New flight.
  • The client's version, X-Plane's version while X-Plane is connected, and the gateway's version, and the light/dark theme button.

docs.title: The services row
docs.text:
Three pills show what the client is connected to:

Pill What it shows Gateway The connection to ATC. Click it for the reason of the last change and Reconnect, which reopens the connection on the same flight X-Plane Connected or not. It turns amber and reads X-Plane: paused while the sim is paused: ATC is silent then and does not hear you Sign-in Green when signed in, red when not (with Sign in), amber when signed in but the sign-in service cannot be reached

docs.title: The radios
docs.text:
COM1 and COM2, active and standby, exactly as X-Plane has them, with the name of the facility on each frequency when ATC knows it ("Seattle Ground").

  • TX marks the radio selected to transmit on your aircraft's audio panel. It turns red while you transmit.
  • ⇄ swaps active and standby, like the flip-flop key on a real radio.
  • A radio tuned to an ATIS says so: "KSEA ATIS Charlie · looping".

The client changes X-Plane's radios and nothing else, so the window always shows what X-Plane really has.

docs.title: Push-to-talk
docs.text:
The big button. Press and hold to transmit, release to stop. Its hint names the facility you are transmitting to. It works with a mouse or a touch screen, and holding Space does the same while the window has focus. If the window loses focus the button releases, so the radio cannot get stuck keyed.

For a button on your yoke or joystick, see Settings.

docs.title: Read back, and Next
docs.text:
Under push-to-talk:

  • Read back: what ATC is still waiting for you to read back, with how long it has waited. It empties when your readback is accepted.
  • Next: after a handoff ("contact Portland Approach one two four point three five") it shows Next: Portland Approach 124.350 with COM1 and COM2 buttons. They put the frequency in that radio's standby; then press ⇄.

docs.title: Last ATC
docs.text: Who spoke last and what they said, with the verdict on your last readback: ✓ Readback accepted or ✗ Corrected. Numbers are shown as you would write them ("119.2"), while the audio says them as a controller does ("one one niner point two").

docs.title: The card slot
docs.text:
One card at a time, picked with the chips above it. The slot keeps its height, so the log below never jumps.

Card When it shows Frequencies Always available: the ATC stations for your flight Approach When ATC starts vectoring you for an approach Parking When ATC asks you to say your parking PDC After you request a pre-departure clearance by text Pilot deviation When ATC flags a deviation, such as taking off without a clearance. It stays until you dismiss it Unable to access data When ATC cannot read its airport data. The client pauses X-Plane; see Troubleshooting

An alert takes the front and its chip turns amber. Hide folds the slot down to its chips.

docs.title: Frequencies
docs.text:
The stations ATC has for your flight, grouped by airport, your departure and destination first. C1 and C2 mark what COM1 and COM2 are tuned to, TX the one you transmit on, and each ATIS shows its current letter.

Each station has two small buttons, 1 and 2: they put its frequency into COM1's or COM2's standby. Then press that radio's ⇄. The list follows the flight: when a clearance or a handoff names another frequency, the card changes with it.

docs.title: The log
docs.text:
Everything that happened, newest at the bottom:

  • You: what the speech recognition heard, in grey while it is still working. A correct readback gets silence on the radio, so the verdict appears here: a green ✓ Readback accepted or an amber ✗ Corrected.
  • ATC: the station, what it said and the frequency. If you were not tuned to it, the next line says it was not played.
  • No reply: why ATC did not answer. See Troubleshooting.
  • Timing: how long each step of the reply took.

Scroll up to read something and the log stays where you left it; scroll back to the bottom and it follows again.

docs.title: Dialogs you will meet
docs.text:
• The startup dialog, each time the client starts: your sign-in, the gateway and X-Plane. It closes by itself when the first two are ready. After a client restart mid-flight it offers Rejoin last flight.
  • New flight: the flight plan, by hand or from SimBrief.
  • The recording question, the first time you connect: see Your data.
  • The approach diagram, full size, when ATC's plan starts and the card is too small to read.

docs.title: The approach plan
docs.text: When ATC vectors you for an approach, you fly one heading at a time. The window shows you the whole plan: where ATC means to take you, and where you are on it.

docs.title: The confirmation in the header
docs.text:
While ATC has you on an approach, the top line of the window says so, beside your callsign:

You see It means ILS · RWY 10R · ATC is vectoring you (blue) ATC has a plan for you and is calling each turn. You do not need to ask for vectors ILS · RWY 10R · cleared for the approach (green) ATC has cleared you for the approach

The badge is the kind of approach: ILS, RNAV, Visual, or another kind by its name, such as LOC.

It shows in both views, whatever card is in the card slot.

docs.title: The Approach card
docs.text:
ATC's plan for a vectored ILS, full size: a left downwind, the base turn at 10.8 nm, joining the final at 8.2 nm, outside the final approach fix.

The diagram is drawn course up: the runway is at the top and the final approach course runs down the page.

  • The runway and the extended centerline, with a tick every 5 nm.
  • The final approach fix, with its name (when the data has one) and its distance from the runway.
  • Where you join the final, with its distance.
  • The path ATC plans, as a dotted line: the downwind, the base turn, the turn to final.
  • Your aircraft, turned to its heading.

Beside the diagram:

  • the plan in one line: "ILS RWY 10R · left downwind · base turn 10.8 nm · join 8.2 nm · FAF 4.8 nm",
  • where you are: "You: 5.0 nm out, 3.0 nm left of the final",
  • the airport, the controller and your assigned altitude,
  • the badge: vectors, then cleared.

A prediction, not a clearance

The card shows ATC's plan. It changes as ATC changes it. Fly the headings and altitudes ATC gives you on the radio, not the picture.

docs.title: Reading it
docs.text:
• Far from the airport, your aircraft sits at the edge of the diagram with its distance, and an arrow points to where it really is. The plan stays large enough to read.
  • Without X-Plane connected, the plan still shows, and the card says your position is not known.
  • As you fly the pattern, the parts behind you drop off, and the dotted line always starts at your aircraft.

docs.title: Bigger
docs.text:
The card slot is small. Bigger opens the diagram in the full window, and Close, Esc or a click outside it closes it again.

If the window is too short for the card's diagram to be readable, the full-size diagram opens by itself when ATC's plan starts. It does so once per approach: after you close it, ATC's updates do not bring it back. Holding Space still transmits while it is open.

docs.title: Turning it off
docs.text:
• Close on the card hides it until ATC plans a different approach.
  • Settings > Display > Show the Approach card turns the card off for good. The confirmation in the header stays.

docs.title: Parking
docs.text:
When ATC asks you to "say parking", the window shows what you can answer.

It happens with Approach at a large airport, with Tower after you leave the runway, or with Ground on the taxi-in. The Parking card comes to the front of the card slot.

docs.title: What you can say
docs.text:
• Names, as big buttons first: "Atlantic Aviation", "FBO", "GA". These are the names a pilot would say on the radio.
  • Gates and stands, grouped by kind: airline gates by concourse, general aviation, cargo, and the rest. A large airport gets a search box.

Tap one and the card copies the words to say: "parking Atlantic Aviation". Then say them on the radio. Picking something in the window sends nothing to ATC: you still ask by voice.

The card goes away once ATC has your parking, when the flight ends, or with Close.

docs.title: The parking map
docs.text:
The parking map, opened full size, on demo scenery: the stands that fit a C172, one of them taken, and your own aircraft taxiing in.

Above the lists, the card draws your destination from your own X-Plane scenery:

  • the runways with their numbers and the taxiways with their letters,
  • every stand as an arrow pointing the way the nose goes,
  • your aircraft, when you are at or near the airport.

Stands that take your kind of aircraft (piston, turboprop, jet or heavy jet, as the scenery lists them) are blue. Only stands for your type, on by default, hides the others. A stand that another aircraft in your X-Plane is sitting on is grey and says taken. You can still pick it, and ATC may tell you it is occupied.

Drag, scroll or pinch to zoom; stand names appear once you are zoomed in. The buttons above the map jump to the ramps that have stands for you. Bigger map opens it in the full window.

Tap a stand, on the map or in the list, and the card shows its name, its kind, whether it is free, and the words to say, with Copy the words.

Everything on the map comes from the X-Plane files on your PC and works offline.

docs.title: What Ground does with it
docs.text:
• A parking you name is where the taxi-in ends: a gate, an FBO by name, or "general aviation".
  • Name nothing and Ground picks a general parking for you.
  • If Ground cannot find what you named, it says so and taxis you somewhere sensible.

docs.title: Pre-departure clearance by text
docs.text: At a busy airport, airline crews often get their IFR clearance as text instead of copying it by voice. You can do the same.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
1. Start your flight. Once ATC is connected, a Request PDC chip shows above the card slot.

  2. Press it. The clearance arrives as the PDC card and in the log:

    N547GA CLRD TO KPDX VIA SUMMA2 THEN AS FILED. MAINT 5000, EXP 16000 10 MIN AFT DEP.
DEP FREQ 119.2. SQUAWK 4521. ATIS K.

  3. Set the squawk and note the departure frequency. There is no voice readback.

  4. When you are ready to taxi, call Ground with the ATIS. You do not need to say "with the PDC".

docs.title: If you cannot get one
docs.text: The card says why, and you call Clearance Delivery by voice instead.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Close takes the card out of the slot. The clearance stays in the log.
  • New flight clears it.
  • The chip shows only while a PDC is possible: ATC connected, and no PDC answer already showing.

docs.title: Your X-Plane's data
docs.text: ATC uses the FAA's published data for everything in the air over the US: procedures, fixes, airways, frequencies, tower hours, airspace and minimum altitudes. On the ground, it uses your X-Plane, so that the taxiways and stands ATC names are the ones you see.

docs.title: ATC asks, the client answers
docs.text:
Nothing is uploaded in advance. When ATC needs something only your X-Plane has, it asks, and the client answers over the flight's connection:

What When From The airport's ground layout: taxiways with their names, hold lines, stands, runways as drawn, runway-use rules The departure airport at the start, the destination when you are inbound The scenery pack that wins in your X-Plane, in scenery_packs.ini order Parking stands When ATC asks you to say parking The same scenery Outside the US only: the airport's runways, frequencies and procedures, the fixes and airways along your route At the start of the flight Your X-Plane's navigation data. It is assumed to be current

It is done safely. ATC can ask only for these kinds of data, for an airport identifier that is checked first. It can never name a file to read. The log says what was read: "ATC read KBFI's ground layout from your X-Plane".

If your scenery has no taxiway data for an airport, Ground says "taxi at your own discretion".

docs.title: The scenery index, once
docs.text: The first flight after installing reads the header of every airport file in your scenery, once, before it connects to ATC. The New flight dialog shows "Preparing the scenery index (one time)…" with a progress bar. On a slow disk this takes a minute or more. Afterwards only new or changed scenery is read.

docs.title: What the client sends during a flight
docs.text:
About once a second, and at once when you change a radio:

  • your aircraft's position, altitude, speed, heading and whether it is on the ground,
  • your radios: frequencies and which one you transmit on,
  • the weather at the aircraft,
  • X-Plane's clock, so that ATC judges things like tower opening hours by the sim's time,
  • the other aircraft X-Plane knows about (its AI traffic, and aircraft a multiplayer plugin adds): the nearest 32.

See Your data for the whole picture.

docs.title: FAA procedures for your X-Plane
docs.text:
Optional. ATC clears you on the FAA's current procedures. If your X-Plane's navigation data is older, your aircraft's FMS may not have a procedure ATC names. Settings > X-Plane data can install the FAA's current procedures into X-Plane, so that the two agree.

  • Check for update shows the release, its AIRAC cycle and its dates.
  • Install downloads it, checks every file, backs up anything it replaces, and writes the FAA's procedure file into your X-Plane's Custom Data folder.
  • Update replaces an installed pack with a newer one.
  • Remove puts your own files back exactly as they were.

You need a flight started to check or install, because the download link comes from ATC. Restart X-Plane afterwards: it reads navigation data only when it starts.

It overrides your navigation data for US procedures

While the pack is installed, X-Plane uses the FAA's procedures in place of your provider's (Navigraph, for example) for the airports it covers. Remove undoes it. The tab warns you when your navigation data is a different AIRAC cycle from the pack: fixes may then not match.

A pack for a cycle that has not started yet can be installed early. The tab marks it Not valid until its first day.

docs.title: What ATC can do
docs.text:
xatc-agent staffs every position of an IFR flight. Each controller is on its real frequency, hands you to the next one at the right place, and uses the phraseology of the FAA's controller handbook (JO 7110.65).

Position What it does for you Clearance Delivery Your IFR clearance, amendments, and a pre-departure clearance by text Ground Pushback, taxi to the runway, runway crossings, progressive taxi, taxi-in to your parking Tower Line up and wait, takeoff and landing clearances, go-arounds, the runway exit Departure and Center Radar contact, climbs, turns on course, direct routings, descents, holds, diversions Approach The approach to expect, vectors to final, ILS, RNAV and visual approach clearances

And at every position:

  • Readbacks are checked, and reminded when you forget one.
  • ATIS and weather come from the weather in your X-Plane.
  • Common requests work everywhere: say again, radio checks, questions, emergencies.

docs.title: The rules it plays by
docs.text:
IFR only, for now. VFR departures, pattern work and flight following are not built yet.

Any US airport. Positions, frequencies, procedures, airspace and minimum altitudes come from the FAA's published data. Taxiways and parking stands come from your own X-Plane scenery. Outside the US, ATC asks your X-Plane for the airport's procedures and frequencies too.

Nobody on a frequency, no reply. Tune a frequency no controller uses and you hear nothing. Tune an ATIS frequency and you hear the broadcast.

It will not make things up. Every clearance is checked against the airport's data and your flight before it is spoken. When you ask for something ATC has not been taught, the answer is fixed:

"November five four seven Golf Alpha, unable, I have not completed that training."

When the answer is no, ATC says why: "unable, runway one niner not available", "continue holding short, traffic".

ATC calls you first when a real controller would: handoffs, a readback you owe, traffic, drifting off your altitude or your taxi route, a go-around.

One reply per call. Ask for two things in one transmission and you get one reply that covers both.

Silent while paused. While X-Plane is paused or in a replay, ATC says nothing and does not hear you.

docs.title: Not built yet
docs.text:
• VFR: departures, pattern work, flight following.
  • A sidestep to a parallel runway (for now: a go-around).
  • Block altitudes and other less common requests. ATC answers "unable, I have not completed that training".
  • Full emergency handling: vectors to the nearest airport, lost-communication routings. The first steps are there.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text: Approach brings you from the arrival to the final approach course and clears you for the approach.

docs.title: Check-in: what to expect
docs.text:
On your first call, Approach gives you the altimeter, your descent, and the approach to expect:

"November five four seven Golf Alpha, Portland Approach, descend and maintain four thousand, expect ILS runway one zero right."

Approach also checks that you have the destination's current ATIS: "confirm you have information Kilo".

docs.title: Which approach
docs.text:
Approach picks from what the airport publishes for the runway in use: the ILS first, then RNAV (GPS), then a localizer approach. In good weather it is a visual approach.

You can ask for the one you want: "request the RNAV runway one zero right", "request vectors for the ILS". You can also ask for another runway and be vectored for it.

docs.title: Vectors to final
docs.text:
Approach vectors you on a downwind, a base and an intercept heading, as a real controller does for a vectored ILS. You do not need to ask for the next turn: ATC calls each one.

  • The first vector says why you are being vectored: "turn left heading two eight zero, descend and maintain four thousand, vectors for the ILS runway one zero right". ATC does not announce the pattern it plans: the Approach card draws it.
  • Altitudes step down as the minimum altitudes allow.
  • Every heading allows for the wind.
  • Coming off a STAR: "depart Battle Ground heading one one zero, descend and maintain five thousand, vectors for the ILS runway one zero right".

The window shows this as it happens: the Approach card draws ATC's plan with your aircraft on it, and the top line of the window says ATC is vectoring you.

docs.title: The approach clearance
docs.text:
The last turn comes with the clearance:

"November five four seven Golf Alpha, turn left heading two five five, maintain three thousand until established, cleared ILS runway one zero right approach."

Read back the heading, the altitude and the approach with its runway. The intercept is 30 degrees or less, at or below the glideslope. A jet is asked to keep 170 knots to the final approach fix.

Approach then hands you to Tower before the final approach fix.

docs.title: Visual approaches
docs.text:
"November five four seven Golf Alpha, field is at your two o'clock, one two miles, report field in sight."

Report the field in sight and you are cleared for the visual approach. If you have not reported it by about 10 nm, Approach gives you the ILS instead. When you report traffic in sight, it may be "number two, follow the Boeing on a five mile final, cleared visual approach".

docs.title: Sequencing and the missed approach
docs.text:
• Behind other traffic on final, Approach slows you ("reduce speed to one eight zero"), extends your downwind, or holds you.
  • After a go-around, Approach gives you a heading, an altitude and vectors for another approach. You can ask to divert instead.
  • Parking. At a large airport Approach may ask you to "say parking" with the approach clearance, so that Tower can pick the best runway exit. The window's Parking card shows what you can say.
  • Cancel IFR near the field: "IFR cancellation received, contact Portland Tower".

docs.title: ATIS and weather
docs.text: ATC's weather is the weather in your X-Plane.

docs.title: The ATIS
docs.text:
Tune an airport's ATIS frequency on COM1 or COM2 and the recording loops, starting mid-broadcast like the real thing. Tune away and it stops. ATC's calls and your own transmissions come first; the loop picks up again after them.

It gives the information letter, the time, the wind, visibility, the sky, temperature, the altimeter, and the runways and approach in use.

  • The letter starts at a random one and advances when the weather changes.
  • The sky comes from X-Plane's cloud layers: "few", "scattered", "broken" or "overcast" with the height, and the ceiling named ("ceiling niner hundred overcast").
  • Gusts are reported when the gust is 10 knots or more over the steady wind.
  • Wind shear in your X-Plane weather becomes "wind shear reported", in the ATIS and in Tower's takeoff and landing clearances.

The window names the ATIS on the radio tuned to it ("KSEA ATIS Charlie · looping"), tags each ATIS in the Frequencies card with its current letter, and puts the full text in the log while you listen.

docs.title: The letter on the radio
docs.text: Say the letter on your first call: "with information Charlie". ATC remembers it for that airport. When the letter has changed since, ATC asks: "confirm you have information Kilo, altimeter three zero zero two". Arriving, Approach checks the destination's letter.

docs.title: Weather in clearances
docs.text:
• Ground gives the wind and the altimeter with your taxi if you did not report the ATIS.
  • Tower gives the wind with every takeoff and landing clearance.
  • Radar controllers give the altimeter when you check in and when you start down.
  • The runway in use follows the wind. A wind shift can change the runway while you taxi, and Ground then gives you a new route.

docs.title: Where the weather comes from
docs.text: The client sends the weather at your aircraft about every five seconds: wind, pressure, temperature, visibility, gusts, wind shear and cloud layers. For an airport you are not at yet, ATC uses X-Plane's regional weather as its estimate. Nothing is fetched from the real world, so ATC always agrees with what you see out of the window.

docs.title: Clearance Delivery
docs.text: Your first call of an IFR flight.

docs.title: The IFR clearance
docs.text:
Call with your callsign, your destination and the ATIS letter. Clearance Delivery reads the clearance in the usual order:

  • the clearance limit (your destination),
  • the route: a SID or radar vectors, "then as filed",
  • the altitude: the initial altitude and the one to expect,
  • the departure frequency,
  • the squawk, different for each flight.

"November five four seven Golf Alpha, cleared to Portland via the Summa Two departure, then as filed. Maintain five thousand, expect one six thousand one zero minutes after departure. Departure frequency one one niner point two, squawk four five two one."

Read all of it back. A correct readback gets "readback correct"; a wrong item is corrected.

You say What happens "Say again the clearance" It is repeated word for word You filed no cruise altitude ATC asks "say requested altitude" before it clears you You filed a SID that serves the runway in use You are cleared on it Your filed route cannot be flown as it is A full route clearance, instead of "then as filed"

docs.title: Amendments
docs.text: When something changes before you depart, Clearance Delivery amends the clearance and says only the items that changed: a new SID, altitude or squawk. Read those back.

docs.title: A clearance by text (PDC)
docs.text: Instead of copying the clearance by voice, press Request PDC in the window. The clearance arrives as text and needs no readback. See Pre-departure clearance by text.

docs.title: One frequency, one controller
docs.text: At many smaller towered airports, one controller works Clearance Delivery and Ground on the same frequency. There the clearance and the taxi come from the same voice, and you are never told to "contact Ground" on the frequency you are already on. Read back your clearance and add "ready to taxi", and you get "readback correct" and your taxi instructions in one reply.

docs.title: Departure and Center
docs.text: The radar controllers: Departure takes you from the runway into the climb, Center takes you to cruise and back down, and each hands you to the next at the edge of its airspace.

docs.title: Departure
docs.text:
Check in with your altitude. Departure answers "radar contact" with the altimeter and your climb:

"November five four seven Golf Alpha, Seattle Departure, radar contact, climb and maintain one six thousand."

On a SID with altitude restrictions it is "climb via the Summa Two departure", sometimes "except maintain" an altitude.

On course. After a heading off the runway, Departure turns you toward your route: "turn left heading two niner zero, vectors to Mapel", then "proceed direct Mapel" on its own. A SID that ends on a heading is followed by "proceed direct" its next fix. You can also ask: "request on course".

Still on the wrong frequency? If you call Tower when you should be with Departure: "you're on Seattle Tower, contact Seattle Departure". If you never check in, Departure asks "are you with me?"

docs.title: Center
docs.text: The handoff to Center comes on its own, near the top of Departure's airspace. Check in and Center clears you to your cruise altitude, in steps around traffic if it has to.

docs.title: What you can ask for
docs.text:
You ask for What you get Higher or lower Your altitude, or "unable" with the reason. With no altitude named: "say requested altitude" Direct to a fix "proceed direct Helns", for a fix ahead on your route A heading or a speed Approved when it is safe A deviation around weather "deviation twenty degrees left approved, advise when able to proceed direct Helns" A hold "hold west of Battle Ground as published, expect further clearance two one three five" A diversion "cleared to the Olympia airport via direct, maintain ..." To return to your departure airport Radar vectors back, and what to expect To cancel IFR "IFR cancellation received, squawk VFR, frequency change approved"

ATC never clears you below the minimum altitude for where you are. The FAA's minimum vectoring and minimum IFR altitude charts for the whole US are in its data.

docs.title: The descent
docs.text:
At the top of descent Center starts you down without being asked:

"November five four seven Golf Alpha, descend via the Helns Six arrival, Portland altimeter three zero zero two."

or a crossing restriction: "cross Battle Ground at and maintain one one thousand". Asking "request lower" or "request descend via" starts the same descent.

Center then hands you to the next sector, and finally to Approach, about 40 nm from the destination or at the end of the arrival.

docs.title: The radar controller calls you
docs.text:
• Altitude: 300 ft off your assigned altitude and not correcting, "verify altitude".
  • Course: "verify on course", "verify you are proceeding direct Helns", or a heading back to your route.
  • A missed restriction on a SID or STAR: "verify you are descending via the Helns Six arrival".
  • Low altitude alert: "low altitude alert, check your altitude immediately, the minimum altitude in your area is ...".
  • Traffic: converging aircraft are called with the clock position, distance, direction and altitude.
  • Speed: above 250 knots below 10,000 ft, "reduce speed to two five zero knots".
  • A readback you owe for an altitude, a crossing or a procedure, about 30 seconds after ATC stops talking.

docs.title: At every position
docs.text: Things you can say to any controller, and things any controller may say to you.

docs.title: Common requests
docs.text:
You say You get "Say again" The last transmission again "Radio check" "November five four seven Golf Alpha, Seattle Ground, read you five" A question The answer, for: the wind, the altimeter, the runway to expect, the ATIS, your assigned heading, altitude or squawk, any facility's frequency, the time, a distance, traffic "Thanks for the help", "good day" One short reply, or a "good day" after a handoff

A remark that needs no answer gets none.

docs.title: Frequency changes
docs.text:
"November five four seven Golf Alpha, contact Seattle Ground one two one point seven."

Reading it back is optional. The window shows Next: Seattle Ground 121.700 with buttons to put it in a radio's standby.

docs.title: Squawk and altimeter
docs.text: Any controller may give you a squawk, "squawk and ident", "ident", or the local altimeter.

docs.title: Traffic and safety alerts
docs.text:
• Traffic advisories: "traffic, two o'clock, five miles, southbound, a Boeing 737, one thousand feet above you". The traffic is the other aircraft in your X-Plane.
  • Safety alerts: a low altitude alert, or a traffic alert with a suggested escape.
  • A TCAS resolution advisory: tell ATC, and it answers "roger" and issues nothing until you report "clear of conflict".

docs.title: Emergencies
docs.text:
The first steps are built:

  • "Mayday", "Pan-Pan" or squawking 7700: "roger, say fuel remaining and souls on board", and you get priority.
  • Lost communications (7600), or no answer after "are you with me?": "if you hear this transmission, ident".

Vectors to the nearest airport and lost-communication routings are not built yet.

docs.title: Pilot deviations
docs.text: When you do something a real controller would report, such as taking off without a clearance or crossing a runway you were told to hold short of, ATC tells you on the radio and the window shows a red Pilot deviation alert until you dismiss it. It is there so you notice, and so the flight can be reviewed afterwards. Nobody will ask you to copy a phone number.

docs.title: When the flight ends
docs.text:
ATC ends the flight by itself when:

  • you are parked with the engines off,
  • the aircraft crashed,
  • X-Plane has been closed for 30 seconds,
  • or you press End flight.

After that nothing reconnects until you press New flight.

docs.title: What ATC says when it cannot
docs.text:
• Not possible: "unable", with the reason.
  • Not taught yet: "unable, I have not completed that training". Each of these is logged, so the gaps get filled in the order pilots hit them.

docs.title: Ground
docs.text: Ground moves you between your parking and the runway, on the taxiways of your own X-Plane scenery.

docs.title: Before you taxi
docs.text:
Pushback. Ask for it and Ground approves it, with the direction to face from your stand. No readback is needed.

Where you are. Tell Ground your position by its name in your scenery: "at alpha eleven", "at the FBO". If that is far from where your aircraft is, Ground checks: "verify at gate bravo twelve?"

docs.title: Taxi to the runway
docs.text:
"November five four seven Golf Alpha, runway one six left, taxi via Bravo, hold short of runway one six center."

  • The route follows your scenery's real taxiways and names.
  • Every runway on the way is a hold short, and you read each one back.
  • If you did not report the ATIS, Ground gives you the wind and the altimeter.
  • If your scenery has no taxiway data for the airport, Ground says "taxi to runway one six left at your own discretion".

Runway crossings are cleared one runway at a time, once the runway is clear. Stop at the hold line and Ground clears you across without being asked.

docs.title: Requests while you taxi
docs.text: You ask for What happens Another runway A new route to it A route "via Alpha" The route goes that way when it can An intersection departure Approved, with the runway distance left Full length A route to the full-length hold line Progressive taxi Ground calls each turn as you come up to it, across the crossings, to the hold line or your parking

docs.title: Ground calls you
docs.text:
• A readback you owe: about 30 seconds after ATC stops talking, "read back hold short instructions".
  • Traffic: "give way to the Airbus", "follow the Boeing", "hold position, traffic".
  • Off your route: "you are off your cleared taxi route", with a new route from where you are.
  • Moving without a clearance: "hold position".
  • A runway change forced by the wind: a new route and the new ATIS letter.
  • At the runway: "contact Tower" or "monitor Tower".

docs.title: Taxi-in after landing
docs.text:
After Tower sends you to Ground, say where you are parking: a gate, an FBO by name, or "general aviation".

  • Name nothing and Ground asks "say parking" once, then picks general parking for you. The window's Parking card lists what you can say.
  • A parking Ground cannot find: "unable to find it, taxi to ..." with the nearest sensible place.
  • A gate that another aircraft is on: you are held on a taxiway until it is free.

docs.title: Readbacks
docs.text: ATC listens to your readback the way a controller does, and the window shows you the verdict.

docs.title: What needs a readback
docs.text:
• An IFR clearance or an amendment: all of its items.
  • Runway instructions: hold short, line up and wait, cleared for takeoff, cleared to land, and each runway crossing.
  • A taxi route's runway and its hold shorts.
  • Altitudes, headings, crossing restrictions, procedures ("descend via"), and an approach clearance with its runway.

A frequency change needs no readback. "Over to Ground", "point seven", or just changing frequency are all fine.

docs.title: A correct readback
docs.text: Silence on the radio, as in real life, and a green ✓ Readback accepted in the window and the log. Only an IFR clearance gets a spoken "readback correct".

docs.title: A wrong readback
docs.text:
ATC corrects the one item that was wrong:

"Negative, squawk six six six two."

The window shows an amber ✗ Corrected. A safety item you left out, such as a hold short or a runway, gets one "read back hold short instructions". ATC asks twice at most, then moves on with a "verify".

docs.title: What it forgives
docs.text:
Speech recognition is not perfect, and neither is anyone's radio work:

  • Only a clearly different value is corrected. An item the recognition did not catch is not held against you, unless it is a safety item (a hold short, a runway, an altitude), which gets one "read back".
  • Names by sound. "Elma five" for the Elmaa Five arrival, "Helms six" for the Helns Six. The number has to be right.
  • Your callsign as you say it. A filed "WALKER 9798" is "Walker ninety-seven ninety-eight". A call with one character off, or with only the end of your registration, still counts as you.
  • Numbers are strict. A different runway, altitude, heading or squawk is never accepted as close enough.

docs.title: When you forget
docs.text:
About 30 seconds after ATC stops talking, and never while you are transmitting, ATC reminds you: "read back hold short instructions", "confirm cleared to land runway one six center". A takeoff clearance is reminded sooner.

The Read back line under push-to-talk shows what ATC is still waiting for, so you can see it before the reminder comes.

docs.title: If ATC did not catch your callsign
docs.text: A garbled call, or one with no callsign, gets "Aircraft calling Seattle Ground, say again." It never gets a clearance.

docs.title: Tower
docs.text: Tower owns the runway: it clears you onto it, off it, and onto it again at the other end of the flight.

docs.title: Departure
docs.text:
Line up and wait when Tower can use the time: never with an arrival close in on your runway.

Takeoff clearance, with the wind (gusts and wind shear when there are any) and where to go after takeoff:

"November five four seven Golf Alpha, wind one six zero at eight, fly heading one six zero, runway one six left, cleared for takeoff."

On an RNAV departure it is "RNAV to" the first fix instead of a heading.

When you have to wait, Tower says why, and clears you without being asked once the reason is gone:

Reason What you hear Traffic on final "hold short of runway one six left, traffic on a two mile final" Wake turbulence behind a heavy "expect departure in two minutes" The runway is occupied Tower holds you, then clears you once it is clear

With an arrival a few miles out, the clearance may be "cleared for takeoff, no delay". Waiting at the line with an arrival further out, Tower may ask "are you ready for an immediate departure?"

Your requests: an intersection departure, a turn-out or a heading after takeoff, "need a few minutes". Another runway or full length sends you back to Ground. If Tower cannot, it says "unable" with the reason. If you say "unable" to a line up and wait or an immediate departure, Tower offers an alternative.

After takeoff, about 1,000 ft above the ground: "contact Seattle Departure".

docs.title: Arrival
docs.text:
Landing clearance, with the wind, your number in the sequence and traffic to follow:

"November five four seven Golf Alpha, wind one seven zero at one zero, runway one six center, cleared to land."

Read back "cleared to land" with the runway. If the runway is not free yet, Tower says "continue" and clears you once it is.

Go-arounds. Tower sends you around when the runway is not clear, and expects one when you call it yourself. You get the missed approach instructions and "contact Approach".

Lined up for the wrong runway? "Confirm you are lined up for runway one six center." Close in, it is a go-around.

The runway exit. On the rollout: "turn left at Mike, hold short of runway one six left". Read it back. Once you are clear of the runway: "contact Ground".

docs.title: Tower calls you
docs.text:
• A takeoff or landing readback you owe: "confirm cleared for takeoff runway one six left".
  • Rolling without a clearance: "stop immediately, I say again, stop immediately".
  • A cancelled takeoff: at low speed "cancel takeoff clearance" with the reason; faster, "stop immediately".
  • A possible pilot deviation, when you took off or landed without a clearance or a readback. The window shows a red alert.

docs.title: What Tower knows about traffic
docs.text: Tower clears takeoffs and landings against the other aircraft in your X-Plane: its AI traffic and aircraft a multiplayer plugin adds. A runway with a departure still on it, or an arrival on short final, is not yours yet. Closely spaced parallel runways are treated as one runway for wake turbulence.
